newsitem.title: FRANCE: French short-dated debt exposed to Dublin deadlock.
newsitem.headline: French short-dated debt exposed to Dublin deadlock.

text.p: The recent sharp convergence between French and German bond yields has left short-dated French bonds particularly vulnerable to any deadlock in stability pact talks, analysts said.

Analysts said convergence over the last two months has left French bond yields below German yields, starting with bonds maturing November 1999, and that the front of the curve would be the first to suffer in the event of any shock.
"If there's a bad surprise, I think the initial reaction would be a sell-off at short end," Ciaran O'Hagan, bond analyst at JP Morgan in Paris, said.
European Union finance ministers will meet tomorrow in Dublin to try to hammer out a deal on the "stability pact" meant to enforce budget rigour on single currency member countries.
"Any prospect of a delay in EMU (economic and monetary union) would make BTANs suffer much more," he said.
He said a shock could lead to both a flattening of the French yield curve and underperformance by short-dated French bonds compared to Germany.
Iain Lindsay, senior bond analyst at Credit Lyonnais, said the short end of the curve would be the first point on the curve to lose relative value against German bonds.

"This second wave of convergence which started towards the end of November was amongst the core group and it has been very much an EMU optimism convergence," Lindsay said. "It needs some justification out of Dublin to make it sustainable."

Eric Chaney, economist at Morgan Stanley in Paris, said while he was worried about a potentially negative impact on French bonds if no agreement were reached in Dublin, domestic investors appeared less concerned.
"French investors appear extremely confident that if there's no agreement in Dublin there will be one in three or six months," Chaney said.
He said a full agreement accepted by all 15 member states appeared could hurt French bonds as it would almost certainly reflect a compromise of tough German demands.
"At the other extreme, a complete failure would certainly hit the French fixed income market, raising serious doubts about EMU itself, while raising hopes of devaluation," Chaney said.
He said the short end of the curve would be hit first.
Analysts said a rigid stability pact of the type advocated by Germany would be the best solution and the weaker the compromise the more likely French bonds would suffer.
"The further it drifts from either the German plan or any outright agreement, the more negative it will be for the market," Lindsay said.

Valerie Plagnol, market economist at Credit Commercial de France said for any agreement to be received favourably by French bonds it would have to include the "notion of serious recession, and a way to implement it".
"I doubt it would be fully automatic, but it would need to be quick and effective," Plagnol said. "If the agreement's not that different from what's already in Maastricht it's not a stability pact."

Irish Prime Minister John Bruton said on Tuesday member states agreed to Germany's call for a numerical definition of economic circumstances which would exempt countries from fines if they stepped over budget deficit limits.
But he left open the possibility of failure in Dublin given that the majority of other member states were not prepared to accept automatic implementation of fines.
